guideTitle: 6 Best Oven Mitts for Cast Iron in 2026
metaTitle: Best Oven Mitts for Cast Iron in 2026
metaDescription: Six oven mitts and gloves compared for cast iron skillets and Dutch ovens, with notes on heat rating, grip, cuff length and why a hot handle stays hot so long.
introParagraphs: Cast iron changes the rules for oven mitts. A skillet pulled from a 450 degree oven has a handle that stays dangerously hot for a long time after the food has been served, because iron stores heat and releases it slowly. The pan is also heavy, often several pounds before any food goes in, so a mitt has to grip as well as insulate. A thin, slippery mitt that is fine for a muffin tin can fail badly here.

We evaluated six picks from product specs and listing details: the GORILLA GRIP silicone mitts at 550 degrees, the HOMWE silicone mitts at 13.7 inches, the Grill Armor fingered gloves at 932 degrees, the FITFIV and Comsmart gloves at 1472 degrees and the KitchenAid Ribbed Soft Silicone pair at 500 degrees. We also looked at a silicone handle cover from Leadiy, which is a different kind of product that deserves a mention but is not ranked here. All ratings come from the listings and should be read as brief-contact limits.

Two decisions drive the choice: whether you want a wide mitt that clamps a helper handle or a fingered glove that lets you pinch a lid knob, and how much stated headroom you want over a hot oven. The sections below take each in turn with named picks.

products.name: GORILLA GRIP Silicone Oven Mitts, 550F
products.description:
For cast iron, the Gorilla Grip reads like a sensible default. The silicone shell is rated to 550 degrees Fahrenheit, which clears the temperature of a skillet that has been preheated in a hot oven, and the cotton lining adds some insulation between the metal and the hand. At 8.3 inches wide, the palm is roomy enough to wrap around a thick helper handle or a Dutch oven bail.

Grip is the point of silicone here. A heavy pan with a slick handle can twist in the hand, and a naturally slip-resistant surface reduces that risk. The waterproof shell is also useful, because cast iron cooking often involves oil, juices and steam, and a wet cloth mitt loses protection fast. The cost is some loss of feel, so it takes care to fit a thumb around a small lid knob.

Compared with the KitchenAid Ribbed at 500 degrees, the Gorilla Grip adds 50 degrees and an inch more palm width. Compared with the HOMWE, it is wider but shorter in the cuff. If one mitt has to do skillet duty and everything else, this is it.
products.bestFor: Heavy skillets and Dutch ovens that need a wide, grippy mitt.
pros: Wide 8.3 inch palm wraps thick handles
cons: Reduced feel for small lid knobs
Cuff is shorter than the HOMWE

products.name: HOMWE BPA-Free Silicone Oven Mitts, 13.7 Inch
products.description:
HOMWE gives you 13.7 inches of mitt, a thick cotton liner and a waterproof silicone shell rated to 500 degrees. That length matters with cast iron because the skillet sits low in the oven and the arm travels over the rack edge to reach it. A cuff that clears the wrist keeps the forearm away from the hot oven frame while you lift.

The 500 degree figure is the same as the KitchenAid, and it is adequate for most skillet work, which sits near 400 to 450 degrees. If you routinely sear in an oven at 500, the margin is thin and a higher-rated pick such as the Gorilla Grip gives more room. The thick liner cushions the hand but fills the inside, so the mitt feels bulky when you need to adjust a grip mid-lift.

This is the pick for a taller cook or anyone who reaches into a deep oven, and for situations where steam rises from a lidded Dutch oven. Against the Grill Armor glove, it trades finger control for sealed coverage.
products.bestFor: Deep ovens and lidded Dutch ovens where steam and reach both matter.
pros: Long 13.7 inch cuff protects the forearm

products.name: Grill Armor Gloves, 932F Oven Gloves with Fingers
products.description:
Grill Armor stands apart as the only fingered glove here that cites an EN407 certification, a European standard for thermal protection, along with a 932 degree Fahrenheit rating. The outer fabric is meta-aramid and para-aramid, the same fibre family behind Nomex and Kevlar, and the inside is lined with cotton. The listing adds that the gloves are cut resistant, which is a bonus if you also use them around a grill grate.

Fingers are the advantage on cast iron. They let you pinch a lid knob, turn a skillet by its tip or slide a pan off a rack, all with a sense of where the metal is. The downside is that fabric takes on moisture, so a skillet that has been soaked or a lid dripping with condensation can wet the glove quickly. The seams between the fingers also have less padding than a thick mitt, so a long hold on a very hot handle is a risk.

The Grill Armor is therefore a precision tool for quick lifts, not a clamp for a long carry. Pair it with a wide mitt such as the Gorilla Grip if you cook with cast iron every day.
products.bestFor: Quick lifts and lid handling where finger control matters.
pros: Aramid fibre handles dry heat well

products.name: FITFIV BBQ Gloves, 1472F
products.description:
FITFIV lists a 1472 degree Fahrenheit test maximum and builds the glove with non-slip silicone on the outside and a hanging loop on the cuff. For cast iron that outdoor heritage is handy: campfire skillets, grill-top Dutch ovens and wood-fired setups produce temperatures that dwarf a kitchen oven, and a glove designed for a barbecue handles them with margin.

The 1472 figure is a material limit, not a promise about how long you can hold a pan, and the listing offers no more context than that. Silicone strips give the grip a bite on a smooth iron handle, and the glove is easy to rinse or machine wash. It is less protective against a boiling splash than a solid silicone mitt, so keep it for dry heat.

Compared with the Comsmart, which lists the same figure, the FITFIV adds a hanging loop that keeps it close at hand. Compared with the Gorilla Grip, it gives finger control at the cost of waterproofing. It is a good second glove for outdoor cast iron.
products.bestFor: Campfire and grill-top cast iron where heat is extreme and dry.
pros: Silicone grip on the outer surface
cons: Rating is a material limit, not hold time
Less padding than a thick mitt

products.name: Comsmart BBQ Gloves, 1472F
products.description:
Comsmart matches the FITFIV on the 1472 degree figure and adds a long cuff that the listing says protects palms, wrists and forearms. The surface is non-slip silicone, and the listing says the gloves are designed to fit most hand sizes, with an inner lining on the cuffs. For cast iron cooked outdoors, the longer sleeve guards the forearm from radiant heat as well as direct contact.

As with the FITFIV, the rating is a material claim without a stated test, so we treat it as a sign of capability rather than permission to hold a hot skillet for a long time. The one-size claim is worth testing: gloves that fit most hands can be loose on small ones, which hurts grip on a heavy pan. A snug fit is safer than a roomy one when the load weighs several pounds.

Compared with the Grill Armor, the Comsmart lacks a named standard but offers a longer cuff. Compared with the HOMWE, it gives fingers and loses sealed coverage. It suits an outdoor cook who sets a skillet on a grate or in coals and needs arm cover.
products.bestFor: Outdoor skillet and Dutch oven cooking where arm cover matters.
cons: No named standard or test context
One size can feel loose on small hands

products.name: KitchenAid Ribbed Soft Silicone Oven Mitt 2-Pack
products.description:
KitchenAid's ribbed silicone pair is rated to 500 degrees Fahrenheit and measures about 7 by 13 inches. The raised ribs give a physical edge to hold against the iron, which helps when you tilt a skillet to pour out a sauce. The listing calls the silicone water resistant and slip resistant, and both are useful on a pan that spits oil.

The 500 degree rating is the lowest in the lineup among the mitts, and the gap over a hot oven is small. For a skillet that spent twenty minutes at 450 degrees, the margin is fine for a brief lift. For anything hotter, or for a long carry across a room, we would reach for the Gorilla Grip first. The mitt is also narrower, so a larger hand may feel snug.

Where it excels is familiarity. A cook who already likes the feel of this pair can use it for cast iron without buying new gear. Compared with the HOMWE, it is shorter by under an inch. Compared with the gloves, it gives sealed protection and no finger control. It is a sound, safe default for ordinary skillet use.
products.bestFor: Cooks who want a familiar brand pair for everyday skillet use.
pros: Ribs give a physical edge on iron handles
cons: Lowest margin over hot oven settings
Narrower palm than the Gorilla Grip

buyingCriteria.criterion: Why cast iron handles stay hot
buyingCriteria.explanation: Iron has a high heat capacity and conducts heat well, so a skillet's handle warms up fully in a hot oven and cools slowly. A handle that was safe to touch on the stovetop can hold well over 400 degrees once it has sat in a 450 degree oven. This means a mitt must be on your hand before you open the oven door, and must stay available for the whole time the pan is hot. The Gorilla Grip at 550 degrees offers the most margin among the silicone mitts here.

A large cast iron skillet can weigh several pounds empty, and a Dutch oven with food far more. A slick mitt on a heavy handle can twist and drop the pan. The Gorilla Grip uses slip-resistant silicone, the KitchenAid uses ribs and the Comsmart and FITFIV add silicone grip strips. Look for texture across the palm and fingers, and test the grip with the pan cold before you rely on it hot.

Many skillets have a short helper handle opposite the long one, and a Dutch oven has two loops. A wide palm wraps these better. The Gorilla Grip is 8.3 inches across, the KitchenAid about 7. A mitt that cannot close around the helper handle forces you to use fingertips, which reduces control and increases the risk of a slip.

Cast iron is often used in deep ovens and with lids that trap steam. The HOMWE at 13.7 inches and the Comsmart's long forearm cuff keep the arm clear of rack edges and rising steam. Opening a lidded Dutch oven releases a burst of hot vapor toward your wrist. Choose a longer cuff for lidded cooking.

Mitt ratings here run from 500 on the HOMWE and KitchenAid to 550 on the Gorilla Grip, with gloves listing 932 on the Grill Armor and 1472 on the FITFIV and Comsmart. A typical cast iron oven session runs 400 to 500 degrees, and a pan preheated for searing can sit near 500. Aim for at least 50 to 100 degrees of headroom over your usual setting. Remember that the gloves rated at 932 and 1472 degrees owe those figures to fabric, while the silicone mitts offer sealed protection against oil.

Silicone cast iron handle covers, such as the Leadiy listing, slip over a skillet handle and are rated lower, with the listing citing 450 degrees as the operating limit. They are useful on the stovetop, where the handle gets warm but not oven-hot, and they should not replace a mitt in the oven. Treat them as a supplement for stovetop work, not an oven tool. Never leave a cover on a handle while the pan goes into the oven unless the listing allows it, because the material may soften or discolor.

howWeEvaluated.title: Heat headroom for iron
howWeEvaluated.description: We compared stated ratings against the temperatures of a preheated skillet. The Grill Armor at 932 and the FITFIV and Comsmart at 1472 lead on paper, the Gorilla Grip at 550 leads among mitts, and the HOMWE and KitchenAid at 500 offer the thinnest margin.

howWeEvaluated.title: Grip on heavy pans
howWeEvaluated.description: We read each listing's grip features, from the Gorilla Grip's slip-resistant silicone to the KitchenAid's ribs and the gloves' silicone strips. Heavy loads reward texture across the whole palm. Grip features were judged by how much of the palm and fingers they cover.

howWeEvaluated.title: Palm and cuff dimensions
howWeEvaluated.description: We looked at stated widths and lengths. The Gorilla Grip's 8.3 inch palm is the widest, the HOMWE's 13.7 inch cuff the longest mitt sleeve, and the Comsmart's long cuff covers the forearm.

howWeEvaluated.title: Steam and splash protection
howWeEvaluated.description: We judged waterproofing for oily, steamy cooking. Silicone mitts scored best, and fabric gloves scored lower because oil and condensation soak into the weave.

howWeEvaluated.title: Control for lids and knobs
howWeEvaluated.description: We considered finger feel for lid knobs and small handles. The Grill Armor, FITFIV and Comsmart gloves lead, and the thick mitts trail. We also noted that a lid knob is small and hot enough to defeat a thick mitt, so a glove or a pinch tool earns a place beside the main mitt.

faq.q: How hot does a cast iron skillet handle get?
faq.a: After time in a hot oven, the whole skillet, handle included, reaches roughly the oven temperature. That is why mitts need ratings well above 400 degrees. Keep a mitt or glove on until the pan has cooled for a long while. Even a pan that looks cool can still hold enough heat to cause a burn, so test with the back of a fingertip held a few inches away.

faq.q: Are silicone mitts or gloves better for cast iron?
faq.a: Silicone mitts such as the Gorilla Grip grip heavy pans and resist oil and steam. Gloves such as the Grill Armor give finger control for lids and are better outdoors. Many cooks own one of each.

faq.q: Do I need a handle cover as well?
faq.a: A silicone handle cover, like the Leadiy listing with a 450 degree operating limit, helps on the stovetop where the handle is warm but not oven-hot. It is not a substitute for a mitt in the oven. Use it as a convenience, not a safety plan. Check the cover's rating against your stovetop use, since a flame licking up the side can exceed it.

faq.q: Why does the handle stay hot so long?
faq.a: Iron stores a lot of heat and releases it slowly, so the handle stays hot well after the pan leaves the heat. A good habit is to leave a mitt draped over the handle as a reminder. Never assume a quiet pan is a cool pan.

faq.q: Is a higher glove rating better for cast iron?
faq.a: More headroom is good, but the rating describes brief contact. The Grill Armor lists 932 and the Comsmart 1472, but you should still lift and set down quickly. Grip and fit matter as much as the number. A tight, grippy fit is safer than a loose glove with a bigger number.

faq.q: Can I use cloth mitts with cast iron?
faq.a: Dry, thick cloth works for a quick lift, but liquid in the fabric passes heat quickly. Silicone mitts such as the HOMWE handle oil and steam better. Avoid thin or damp cloth.

faq.q: How do I carry a hot Dutch oven safely?
faq.a: Use two hands, a wide mitt on each, and clear the path before you lift. The Gorilla Grip's wide palm wraps the loop handles well. Set the pot down on a trivet, not directly on a counter. Keep a second mitt nearby for steadying the lid, and lift lids away from your face.
